sections.title: Clinical pattern
sections.text: Recurrent migraine attacks can combine severe headache, nausea, and light or sound sensitivity; unilateral pain is common but not universal.

sections.title: Acute treatment
sections.text: VA/DoD recommends specified triptans, including sumatriptan, for acute migraine; check contraindications.

sections.title: Secondary headache warnings
sections.text: Thunderclap onset, focal neurologic findings, fever, papilledema, or major pattern change warrant secondary-cause assessment.

sections.title: Additional referenced study applications
sections.text: Frequent headache painkiller use can contribute to rebound headache. Preventive treatment aims to reduce attacks rather than only relieve an attack already underway.

choices.text: Tension-type headache
Cluster headache
Medication withdrawal
Migraine
Acute sinusitis

questions.explanation: The headache with nausea and sensory sensitivity supports migraine.

distractorExplanations.B: This lacks the typical cluster pattern.
distractorExplanations.C: No withdrawal is described.

distractorExplanations.C: Not listed.

distractorExplanations.E: Not migraine treatment.

questions.stem: A learner reviews a fictional patient with established migraine who now takes headache painkillers most days and has increasingly frequent headaches. Which issue deserves assessment before simply increasing rescue use?

choices.text: Possible medication-related rebound headache
Increase the number of rescue-medication days
Assess only whether each rescue dose reduces pain
Change the rescue product without reviewing use frequency
Defer medication-use review until preventive treatment fails

distractorExplanations.B: That change misses the cited concern about frequent painkiller use.

choices.text: Review only medication used once an attack has started
Discuss preventive treatment with the treating clinician
Increase as-needed rescue use without discussing prevention
Wait for the next attack to reassess current pain
Change only the timing of the acute rescue dose

distractorExplanations.D: The question asks about future attack frequency, not current pain.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish migraine prevention from acute relief.

sections.title: Clinical pattern
sections.text: Tension-type headache is often mild to moderate bilateral pressure, not worsened by routine activity, without nausea or vomiting. Stress and poor sleep may contribute.

sections.title: Chronic prevention
sections.text: VA/DoD suggests amitriptyline for chronic tension-type prevention; consider adverse effects and risks.

sections.title: Reassessment
sections.text: Review frequency and medication use; abrupt severe pain or neurologic changes warrant secondary-headache evaluation.

sections.title: Additional referenced study applications
sections.text: A headache diary can record timing, duration, treatment, sleep, stress, and possible triggers. Stress, inadequate sleep, dehydration, and posture can contribute to tension-type headache.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old describes recurrent three-hour mild bilateral pressing headaches after stressful shifts and poor sleep. Walking or climbing stairs does not worsen the pain. There is no nausea, vomiting, aura, or light or sound sensitivity. Which primary headache pattern is most likely?

choices.text: Cluster headache
Migraine with aura
Trigeminal neuralgia
Tension-type headache
Subarachnoid hemorrhage

questions.explanation: Bilateral pressure without nausea or activity aggravation favors tension-type.

distractorExplanations.A: No severe clustered attacks.
distractorExplanations.B: No aura or typical migraine-associated features.
distractorExplanations.C: No brief focal facial attacks.
distractorExplanations.E: No abrupt severe emergency pattern.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize a likely tension-type presentation.

choices.text: Amoxicillin
Donepezil
Amitriptyline
Levetiracetam
Clopidogrel

questions.explanation: Recommendation 25 suggests amitriptyline for chronic tension-type prevention.

distractorExplanations.A: Not headache prevention.
distractorExplanations.B: Not headache prevention.
distractorExplanations.D: Not suggested here.
distractorExplanations.E: Not headache prevention.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a supported chronic tension-type preventive.

questions.stem: An adult in a study vignette has recurrent tension-type headaches but cannot identify a pattern. Which follow-up tool best helps characterize possible triggers and treatment response?

choices.text: Track only headache severity without timing or context
Track only the number of pain-reliever tablets used
Record headache timing, duration, treatment, sleep, and stress
Track sleep duration without recording headache episodes
Recall only the most severe episode at the next visit

questions.explanation: NIH recommends a headache diary that captures symptoms, timing, treatment, and context to identify patterns.

distractorExplanations.A: Severity alone omits trigger and treatment information needed here.
distractorExplanations.B: Medication count alone does not characterize symptom context or response.
distractorExplanations.D: Sleep may matter, but this does not link sleep to headache patterns.
distractorExplanations.E: Retrospective recall of one episode misses the recurring pattern.

questions.learningObjective: Use a headache diary to characterize patterns.

questions.stem: A fictional patient has tension-type headaches during weeks of poor sleep, little fluid intake, and prolonged desk work. Which counseling topic is supported alongside appropriate clinical review?

choices.text: Focus only on increasing acute pain-reliever use
Review only medication brand preference
Attribute the headaches to desk posture alone
Review sleep, hydration, stress, and posture
Wait for headaches to become constant before reviewing habits

questions.explanation: NIH identifies these modifiable contributors to tension-type headache; the vignette does not establish an infectious cause.

distractorExplanations.A: This does not assess the described modifiable contributors.
distractorExplanations.B: Product preference does not address sleep, hydration, stress, or posture.
distractorExplanations.C: NIH describes several possible contributors; the case includes more than posture.
distractorExplanations.E: The recurrent pattern already provides relevant contributors to review.

questions.learningObjective: Identify modifiable tension-headache contributors.

sections.title: Emergency recognition
sections.text: Sudden unilateral weakness or speech difficulty warrants emergency stroke evaluation; record symptom onset and activate emergency transport.

sections.title: Disabling deficit and reperfusion
sections.text: For eligible disabling ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours, the 2026 guideline supports alteplase or tenecteplase; eligibility remains essential.

sections.title: Disability matters
sections.text: A low NIHSS score alone does not exclude thrombolysis when deficits are disabling. Non-disabling deficits follow a different treatment pathway.

sections.title: Additional referenced study applications
sections.text: When stroke symptoms appear, note their onset and activate emergency services promptly. CDC advises ambulance transport rather than driving oneself or arranging a private ride.

questions.stem: In clinic, a 68-year-old suddenly develops right arm weakness and aphasia. Symptoms began 20 minutes ago. What is the best next action?

choices.text: Schedule next-week review
Activate emergency stroke transport
Observe overnight at home
Start outpatient physical therapy
Obtain routine lipids first

questions.explanation: Acute focal deficits require immediate emergency stroke evaluation.

distractorExplanations.A: Delays time-sensitive evaluation.
distractorExplanations.C: Delays emergency care.
distractorExplanations.D: Does not address the acute event.
distractorExplanations.E: Would delay stroke assessment.

questions.learningObjective: Prioritize emergency evaluation of acute focal deficits.

questions.stem: A stroke team confirms ischemic stroke with disabling aphasia 90 minutes after onset. Hemorrhage and all thrombolysis contraindications are excluded. Which statement matches the 2026 guideline?

choices.text: Tenecteplase is never supported
Only aspirin is appropriate
NIHSS must exceed a fixed cutoff
Wait until 4.5 hours elapse
Either alteplase or tenecteplase is supported

questions.explanation: Eligible disabling stroke supports rapid IV thrombolysis with either agent.

distractorExplanations.A: Both agents are endorsed.
distractorExplanations.B: This ignores disabling deficits.
distractorExplanations.C: Disability matters beyond NIHSS alone.
distractorExplanations.D: Treatment should be prompt.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the 2026 early thrombolysis recommendation.

questions.stem: A fictional patient develops sudden facial weakness and abnormal speech while a family member watches. Emergency services are being called. Which additional information should the family record immediately?

choices.text: The time emergency personnel are expected to arrive
The time the symptoms will be reassessed
The time of the most recent routine neurologic examination
The time of the next scheduled medical visit
The time the symptoms first appeared

questions.explanation: CDC advises noting symptom onset because the timing informs emergency treatment decisions.

distractorExplanations.A: Arrival time does not establish when symptoms began.
distractorExplanations.B: A planned reassessment time does not establish onset.
distractorExplanations.C: The observed acute onset is the information asked for here.
distractorExplanations.D: The future appointment does not define the current symptom onset.

questions.learningObjective: Record observed stroke symptom onset.

questions.stem: In a study vignette, an adult suddenly develops unilateral weakness and trouble speaking. A relative proposes driving to the emergency department. Which transport plan is recommended by CDC?

choices.text: Call emergency services for ambulance transport
Have the patient drive directly to the hospital
Have the relative arrange private transport after observation
Call the usual clinic first and await a routine callback
Arrange transport only if the symptoms persist

questions.explanation: CDC recommends calling 911 and using an ambulance so emergency personnel can begin care en route.

distractorExplanations.B: CDC advises ambulance transport rather than the affected patient driving.
distractorExplanations.C: This adds observation rather than the recommended immediate emergency response.
distractorExplanations.D: Waiting for a routine callback does not provide the advised emergency transport.
distractorExplanations.E: CDC advises an immediate emergency response to stroke symptoms.

questions.learningObjective: Choose emergency transport for suspected stroke.

sections.title: Resolved symptoms remain important
sections.text: Resolution of a focal deficit does not remove the need for prompt assessment; suspected TIA signals serious stroke risk.

sections.title: Brain imaging
sections.text: The AHA statement prefers MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging for tissue assessment; CT plus CTA offers a practical alternative when needed.

sections.title: Risk assessment and follow-up
sections.text: Disposition combines neurologic evaluation and vessel imaging with risk assessment. Early neurology input is preferable to a score alone.

sections.title: Additional referenced study applications
sections.text: TIA involves a temporary interruption of blood supply to part of the brain and can warn of future stroke. After urgent assessment, prevention includes managing blood pressure and cholesterol and supporting a healthy lifestyle.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old had sudden unilateral weakness and speech difficulty that resolved before arrival. Which response is most appropriate?

choices.text: Reassure because examination normalized
Wait for recurrence
Routine annual follow-up
Treat only if symptoms persist a week
Prompt suspected-TIA evaluation

questions.explanation: Resolved focal symptoms still warrant prompt suspected-TIA evaluation.

distractorExplanations.A: Resolution does not remove stroke risk.
distractorExplanations.B: Would delay evaluation.
distractorExplanations.C: Too delayed for this event.
distractorExplanations.D: Persistence is not required.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize urgency despite symptom resolution.

questions.stem: During a suspected-TIA workup, MRI is immediately available and there is no contraindication. Which test best assesses small ischemic brain tissue lesions?

choices.text: MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging
Plain skull radiographs
Carotid auscultation alone
Routine EEG alone
Lumbar radiographs

questions.explanation: The AHA statement prefers MRI-DWI for brain tissue assessment.

distractorExplanations.B: Does not assess ischemic tissue.
distractorExplanations.C: Cannot assess brain tissue injury.
distractorExplanations.D: Does not identify ischemic tissue.
distractorExplanations.E: Does not assess the brain.

questions.learningObjective: Choose sensitive tissue imaging in suspected TIA.

questions.stem: A fictional patient has completed urgent assessment after a brief episode of unilateral weakness and is diagnosed with TIA. Which mechanism best explains the transient episode?

choices.text: Progressive loss of cortical neurons over years
Briefly blocked blood supply to part of the brain
An episode of abnormal electrical activity in the brain
Compression of a peripheral nerve outside the brain
A disturbance originating in the inner-ear balance system

questions.explanation: The MedlinePlus summary describes a brief blockage of brain blood supply; the alternatives are not established mechanisms for this vignette.

distractorExplanations.A: The cited TIA explanation is a brief interruption of brain blood supply.
distractorExplanations.C: The supplied diagnosis is TIA, with the cited transient ischemic mechanism.
distractorExplanations.D: The source locates TIA’s mechanism in brain blood supply.
distractorExplanations.E: The diagnosed event is explained by transient cerebral blood-supply interruption.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the transient ischemic mechanism.

questions.stem: After urgent evaluation for TIA in a study case, a patient asks what can reduce future stroke risk. Which ongoing plan is supported by the cited summary?

choices.text: Review lifestyle habits but omit blood pressure and cholesterol
Review medications but omit smoking and activity habits
Address blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking, diet, and activity
Focus only on whether neurologic symptoms recur
Delay prevention planning until another episode occurs

questions.explanation: MedlinePlus links TIA with future stroke risk and supports managing vascular risk factors and healthy habits.

distractorExplanations.A: The cited prevention plan includes management of both vascular risks.
distractorExplanations.B: The cited plan also includes healthy lifestyle measures.
distractorExplanations.D: Symptom surveillance alone omits the described risk-reduction measures.
distractorExplanations.E: The evaluated TIA already signals a reason to address future stroke risk.

questions.learningObjective: Identify prevention priorities after evaluated TIA.

sections.title: Aim for seizure control
sections.text: Medication can control seizures for many people. Persistent seizures warrant reassessment; selected patients may need other treatment approaches.

sections.title: Provide safe first aid
sections.text: Protect from nearby hazards, position safely and time the seizure. A seizure lasting more than five minutes requires emergency help; do not restrain or put objects in the mouth.

sections.title: Support adherence and tracking
sections.text: Take antiseizure medicine as prescribed, discuss other drugs and supplements with the clinician, and track seizures and potential triggers.

sections.title: Additional referenced study applications
sections.text: Seizure first aid includes clearing hazards, cushioning the head, and gently positioning the person on their side when appropriate. Do not restrain them or put objects in their mouth. A first-ever seizure warrants emergency help. Food or water should wait until full alertness returns.

questions.stem: An adult has an ongoing generalized convulsive seizure that has lasted six minutes. The area is cleared and the person is positioned safely. What additional action is indicated?

choices.text: Force a spoon into the mouth
Call emergency medical services
Restrain all limb movements
Give water during the convulsion
Wait an hour before seeking help

questions.explanation: CDC advises emergency help when a seizure lasts longer than five minutes.

distractorExplanations.A: Objects in the mouth can injure.
distractorExplanations.C: Restraint can injure.
distractorExplanations.D: Food or water can cause choking.
distractorExplanations.E: The duration already meets the emergency criterion.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the seizure first-aid emergency threshold

questions.stem: A patient with established epilepsy frequently forgets prescribed medication and has difficulty describing breakthrough events. Which plan best supports ongoing management?

choices.text: Stop medication whenever symptoms seem absent
Replace medication with unreviewed supplements
Improve prescribed-dose adherence and keep a seizure record
Take medicine only after a seizure
Discard the event record

questions.explanation: CDC supports taking medication as prescribed and tracking seizures.

distractorExplanations.A: Feeling well does not justify self-discontinuation.
distractorExplanations.B: Supplements should be discussed with the clinician.
distractorExplanations.D: This is not prescribed maintenance use.
distractorExplanations.E: Tracking helps identify patterns.

questions.learningObjective: Use adherence and tracking in epilepsy self-management

questions.stem: During a simulated generalized convulsive seizure, a bystander reaches for a spoon to put between the person’s teeth. Which action best follows CDC first aid?

choices.text: Insert a soft object between the teeth
Hold the limbs firmly to stop the movements
Offer water as soon as the movements slow
Keep objects out of the mouth, clear hazards, and cushion the head
Prioritize opening the jaw instead of clearing nearby hazards

questions.explanation: CDC advises against mouth objects and restraint and recommends protecting the person from nearby hazards.

distractorExplanations.A: CDC advises against placing any object in the mouth.
distractorExplanations.B: CDC advises against restraining the person.
distractorExplanations.C: CDC advises waiting until full alertness before food or water.
distractorExplanations.E: Mouth manipulation is not the recommended protective first-aid action.

questions.learningObjective: Apply safe first aid during convulsions.

questions.stem: A fictional adult has a first-ever convulsive seizure lasting two minutes and begins waking afterward. No established seizure disorder is known. Which response is supported even though five minutes were not reached?

choices.text: Observe without calling solely because the event lasted under five minutes
Wait for a second event before requesting emergency help
Arrange routine follow-up only after the person returns to baseline
Treat the short event as an established familiar seizure pattern
Call emergency services because this was a first-ever seizure

questions.explanation: CDC includes a first-ever seizure among indications for calling 911; duration is not the only criterion.

distractorExplanations.A: First-ever seizure is a separate CDC criterion for emergency help.
distractorExplanations.B: The first-ever event itself meets the cited criterion.
distractorExplanations.C: Return toward baseline does not remove the first-ever-event criterion.
distractorExplanations.D: The vignette supplies no established seizure disorder or familiar pattern.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize a seizure emergency beyond duration.

sections.title: Recognize the positional pattern
sections.text: BPPV produces brief spinning episodes with specific head-position changes. Displaced inner-ear particles disturb vestibular signals.

sections.title: Characterize dizziness carefully
sections.text: Record episode duration, positional triggers, associated hearing symptoms, falls and medicines. Dizziness has multiple possible causes and may warrant specialist assessment.

sections.title: Know the treatment mechanism
sections.text: A trained clinician may use an Epley maneuver to relocate displaced particles in BPPV. Some people need more than one treatment session.

sections.title: Additional referenced study applications
sections.text: Vertigo with hearing loss, tinnitus, and ear fullness warrants assessment for another balance disorder, including Ménière disease. Balance problems also require attention to falls, lighting, handrails, and mobility support. NIDCD separately describes vestibular neuronitis mainly as vertigo, labyrinthitis as inner-ear inflammation/infection, and Mal de Debarquement as rocking after travel.

questions.stem: An adult has brief spinning when rolling over in bed, with no symptoms between episodes. Which listed disorder best fits this pattern?

choices.text: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
Persistent generalized anxiety alone
Chronic insomnia
Carpal tunnel syndrome
Acne vulgaris

questions.explanation: Brief vertigo triggered by a head-position change fits the described BPPV pattern.

distractorExplanations.B: Anxiety alone does not specifically explain this positional pattern.
distractorExplanations.C: Insomnia does not explain the vertigo.
distractorExplanations.D: A wrist neuropathy does not explain this pattern.
distractorExplanations.E: Acne does not explain vertigo.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize a typical BPPV history

questions.stem: A clinician confirms BPPV in a patient suitable for a repositioning maneuver. Which listed intervention addresses the displaced inner-ear particles?

choices.text: Epley maneuver
Antibiotics for every episode
Chronic diazepam as a particle-removing drug
Oral corticosteroids for every episode
Daily aspirin as a particle-removing drug

questions.explanation: The Epley maneuver can relocate particles contributing to BPPV.

distractorExplanations.B: Antibiotics do not mechanically relocate particles.
distractorExplanations.C: Diazepam does not remove the particles.
distractorExplanations.D: Steroids do not mechanically relocate particles.
distractorExplanations.E: Aspirin does not relocate particles.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a particle-repositioning intervention

questions.stem: A study case initially labeled BPPV now includes hearing loss, tinnitus, and a feeling of fullness in one ear during vertigo episodes. Which alternative is specifically described by NIDCD?

choices.text: Ménière disease
BPPV without revisiting the diagnosis
Vestibular neuronitis
Labyrinthitis
Mal de Debarquement syndrome

questions.explanation: NIDCD describes this cluster with Ménière disease; a prior BPPV label should not prevent reassessment.

distractorExplanations.B: The additional hearing-loss, tinnitus, and fullness cluster warrants reassessment.
distractorExplanations.C: The cited neuronitis description centers on vertigo rather than this ear-symptom cluster.
distractorExplanations.D: Ménière disease is the specific match for the cited combined ear symptoms.
distractorExplanations.E: NIDCD describes rocking after travel rather than this combined ear-symptom pattern.

questions.learningObjective: Use associated ear symptoms in vertigo reassessment.

questions.stem: A fictional older adult with a diagnosed balance disorder nearly falls when walking to the bathroom in darkness. Which additional plan is supported alongside condition-specific treatment?

choices.text: Focus only on repeating the condition-specific maneuver
Improve lighting and handrails and assess mobility support
Wait for a completed fall before reviewing home safety
Review dizziness frequency without assessing the walking environment
Recommend mobility support without discussing lighting or handrails

questions.explanation: NIDCD recommends measures such as avoiding dark walking areas, adding handrails, and using support when needed.

distractorExplanations.A: Treatment alone does not address the immediate environmental fall hazard.
distractorExplanations.C: The near-fall already identifies the risk addressed by the source.
distractorExplanations.D: Episode frequency alone omits the hazard described in the case.
distractorExplanations.E: Support may help, but this plan leaves the stated environmental risks unaddressed.

questions.learningObjective: Address fall risk with balance disorders.

sections.title: Do not dismiss symptoms
sections.text: Investigate reported cognitive change. Obtain both the patient's account and collateral information about cognition and everyday function.

sections.title: Assess contributing conditions
sections.text: The initial evaluation includes a focused examination, laboratory assessment and structural brain imaging; MRI is preferred when available and appropriate.

sections.title: Include the care partner
sections.text: Assess understanding and decision-making capacity, then communicate the evaluation and care plan with the patient and an appropriate care partner.

sections.title: Additional referenced study applications
sections.text: Progressive memory problems affecting daily activities are not simply normal aging and merit evaluation. Mild cognitive impairment carries increased concern, but not everyone with MCI develops Alzheimer disease.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old reports increasing memory difficulty. Her daughter describes missed bills over eight months. What best strengthens the initial assessment?

choices.text: Dismiss symptoms as normal aging
Obtain patient and informant histories of cognition and function
Diagnose Alzheimer disease solely from age
Skip assessment because she lives independently
Use a blood biomarker as the entire evaluation

questions.explanation: Collateral functional history is part of the recommended diagnostic assessment.

distractorExplanations.A: Symptoms warrant evaluation.
distractorExplanations.C: Age alone is insufficient.
distractorExplanations.D: Living independently does not exclude impairment.
distractorExplanations.E: A biomarker does not replace the clinical evaluation.

questions.learningObjective: Use collateral history in cognitive evaluation

questions.stem: A patient undergoing an initial dementia evaluation can safely undergo MRI, and MRI is available. Which structural study is preferred?

choices.text: Routine skull radiographs
Carotid auscultation alone
Plain cervical films
No structural imaging
Brain MRI

questions.explanation: MRI is the preferred structural imaging modality in this setting.

distractorExplanations.A: Skull films do not assess brain structure.
distractorExplanations.B: Auscultation is not structural brain imaging.
distractorExplanations.C: Cervical films do not evaluate dementia.
distractorExplanations.D: Structural imaging is part of the evaluation.

questions.learningObjective: Select structural imaging for suspected dementia

questions.stem: A study vignette describes years of worsening memory followed by getting lost in familiar places and difficulty managing daily activities. Which counseling response best reflects the cited summary?

choices.text: Attribute the functional decline to normal aging
Reassure on the basis that the changes occurred gradually
Explain that this exceeds normal aging and needs evaluation
Assess only memory while omitting daily functioning
Diagnose Alzheimer disease from this brief history alone

questions.explanation: MedlinePlus distinguishes progressive functional impairment from normal aging and recommends evaluating noticeable memory changes.

distractorExplanations.A: The cited summary distinguishes AD-type functional decline from normal aging.
distractorExplanations.B: Gradual onset does not make the described functional impairment normal.
distractorExplanations.D: The loss of daily function is a central feature of the case.
distractorExplanations.E: The summary supports evaluation rather than confirmation from this history alone.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize cognitive decline beyond normal aging.

questions.stem: A fictional patient diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment asks whether Alzheimer disease is inevitable. Which response is supported?

sections.title: Acute fluctuating attention
sections.text: Abrupt confusion with impaired attention and changing alertness suggests delirium. A person with dementia can also develop delirium.

sections.title: Identify contributors
sections.text: Evaluate and address underlying illness, medication effects and other contributors. Support orientation, sensory aids, hydration and sleep.

sections.title: Avoid routine sedation
sections.text: For postoperative delirium without threatening agitation, do not routinely give antipsychotics or benzodiazepines. Withdrawal syndromes require a different assessment.

sections.title: Additional referenced study applications
sections.text: Delirium may be hypoactive rather than agitated. A new episode prompts assessment for causes such as medication effects, withdrawal, dehydration, infection, and other illness; correcting the cause is a treatment priority.

questions.stem: An older inpatient was conversant yesterday but now cannot sustain attention. Alertness varies over hours. What best characterizes this change?

choices.text: Normal aging
Stable lifelong intellectual disability
Uncomplicated slowly progressive dementia alone
Delirium
A normal response requiring no assessment

questions.explanation: Acute, fluctuating impairment of attention is characteristic of delirium.

distractorExplanations.A: Normal aging does not explain this abrupt change.
distractorExplanations.B: The onset is newly acute.
distractorExplanations.C: Slow progression alone does not explain hourly fluctuation.
distractorExplanations.E: Delirium requires evaluation.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize delirium from its time course and attention deficit

questions.stem: After surgery, an older adult has quiet delirium without aggression or dangerous behavior. Alcohol and sedative withdrawal are excluded. Which approach is best?

choices.text: Scheduled haloperidol for every delirium case
Long-term diazepam to restore orientation
Investigate causes and provide supportive care
Ignore symptoms until discharge
Restrain the patient routinely

questions.explanation: Cause-directed evaluation and supportive care are appropriate; routine sedating drugs are discouraged here.

distractorExplanations.A: Antipsychotics are not routine treatment in this scenario.
distractorExplanations.B: Benzodiazepines are not first-line here.
distractorExplanations.D: Delirium needs prompt assessment.
distractorExplanations.E: Routine restraint is not the recommended approach.

questions.learningObjective: Manage non-dangerous postoperative delirium

Interpret quiet behavior alone as recovery
Attribute the abrupt change only to established dementia
Assess only nighttime behavior and disregard the daytime change

questions.explanation: MedlinePlus describes hypoactive delirium with reduced activity and sleepiness; agitation is not required.

distractorExplanations.B: A new sleepy, inattentive presentation does not establish recovery.
distractorExplanations.C: The source recognizes an acute delirium process, including in people with dementia.
distractorExplanations.D: The abrupt daytime change remains relevant to delirium assessment.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize a hypoactive delirium presentation.

distractorExplanations.D: The cited treatment priority is identifying and addressing the cause.

questions.learningObjective: Investigate reversible delirium contributors.

sections.title: Select initial treatment
sections.text: For uncomplicated MDD, psychotherapy or antidepressant monotherapy can be selected with patient preference. SSRIs are among supported initial medications.

sections.title: Measure response
sections.text: Track symptoms with a quantitative measure during care. Severe, persistent or recurrent depression may warrant combined psychotherapy and medication.

sections.title: Protect remission
sections.text: After remission with an antidepressant, continue the effective therapeutic regimen for at least six months to reduce relapse risk.

sections.title: Additional referenced study applications
sections.text: VA/DoD suggests quantitative severity measurement during treatment planning and follow-up. It also suggests medication plus evidence-based psychotherapy for severe, persistent, or recurrent MDD; these are conditional recommendations.

sections.title: Persistent difficult-to-control worry
sections.text: GAD involves difficult-to-control worry on most days for at least six months, with associated symptoms and clinically important impact.

sections.title: Offer evidence-based psychotherapy
sections.text: CBT is an established psychotherapy for GAD. Treatment selection depends on the person's needs, preferences and medical situation.

sections.title: Discuss medication tradeoffs
sections.text: SSRIs and SNRIs can treat GAD but take weeks to work. Benzodiazepines can cause tolerance and dependence and may be prescribed only briefly.

sections.title: Additional referenced study applications
sections.text: GAD assessment considers hard-to-control worry over at least six months, associated symptoms, and impact. SSRI/SNRI benefit may take several weeks rather than appearing immediately.

questions.stem: An adult has diagnosed GAD with substantial functional impairment and prefers psychotherapy. Which option has specific support in the NIMH reference?

choices.text: Unstructured reassurance alone indefinitely
Routine brain surgery
Cognitive behavioral therapy
Daily alcohol to induce relaxation
Avoidance of all feared activities as the sole intervention

questions.explanation: CBT is supported by the NIMH treatment reference.

distractorExplanations.A: Reassurance alone is inadequate for the stated impairment.
distractorExplanations.B: Surgery is not a GAD treatment.
distractorExplanations.D: Alcohol is not a recommended treatment.
distractorExplanations.E: Avoidance alone is not evidence-based CBT.

questions.learningObjective: Choose an evidence-based psychological treatment

questions.stem: A patient with GAD requests indefinite daily diazepam because it acts quickly. What concern best explains why this is unsuitable as routine long-term care?

choices.text: Benzodiazepines are antibiotics
They require years before any effect
They cure every anxiety disorder permanently
They are the only effective GAD treatment
They can produce tolerance and dependence

questions.explanation: Tolerance and dependence limit routine long-term benzodiazepine use.

distractorExplanations.A: The drug class is not antibacterial.
distractorExplanations.B: They act rapidly rather than after years.
distractorExplanations.C: They do not guarantee cure.
distractorExplanations.D: Other established treatments exist.

questions.learningObjective: Counsel about long-term benzodiazepine limitations

choices.text: Adjustment disorder
Panic disorder
Social anxiety disorder
Generalized anxiety disorder
Obsessive-compulsive disorder

distractorExplanations.A: The sustained multi-domain worry pattern supports assessing GAD in the cited source.
distractorExplanations.B: The supplied history describes persistent worry rather than establishing this alternative.
distractorExplanations.C: The worry extends across everyday domains rather than establishing this alternative.
distractorExplanations.E: The vignette does not establish this alternative to the cited GAD pattern.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the GAD duration and symptom pattern.

choices.text: Expect the full benefit to be evident after the first dose
Declare the treatment ineffective after two days
Change treatment solely from the absence of immediate relief
Assess only immediate sedation as evidence of effectiveness

distractorExplanations.B: Two days is shorter than the source’s described onset interval.
distractorExplanations.C: The cited onset interval supports follow-up rather than this conclusion alone.
distractorExplanations.D: The source describes delayed symptom benefit, not immediate sedation as the goal.

questions.learningObjective: Set realistic onset expectations for GAD medication.

sections.text: Lithium or quetiapine are suggested for acute mania. Suspected mania during antidepressant treatment warrants a clinical reassessment.

sections.title: Treat bipolar depression specifically
sections.text: Quetiapine monotherapy has a strong recommendation for acute bipolar depression. A unipolar depression treatment plan should not be assumed equivalent.

sections.title: Plan relapse prevention
sections.text: Maintenance choices depend on the episode pattern. Lamotrigine has strong support for preventing recurrence of bipolar depressive episodes.

sections.title: Additional referenced study applications
sections.text: Manic symptoms can include unusually elevated or irritable mood, increased activity, racing thoughts, and decreased need for sleep. Assessment considers the lifetime course; unrecognized bipolar illness can be missed during depression-only visits.

A major depressive episode
Generalized anxiety disorder
A sleep disorder without a mood episode

distractorExplanations.E: The marked change and disrupted function warrant assessment rather than dismissal.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize a manic symptom constellation.

questions.stem: A fictional adult presents during depression and reports previous periods of unusually high energy that felt productive. Which additional history best reduces the risk of missing bipolar illness?

choices.text: Document only depressive symptoms present today
Review lifetime mood episodes, activity changes, severity, and family history
Review sleep only during the current depressive period

sections.title: Prioritize trauma-focused therapy
sections.text: Recommended individual therapies include prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy and EMDR. The guideline favors recommended psychotherapy over medication when feasible.

sections.title: Measure change
sections.text: Use a validated PTSD severity instrument, such as PCL-5, to track response while continuing a clinical assessment.

sections.title: Avoid benzodiazepines for PTSD
sections.text: The guideline recommends against benzodiazepines as PTSD treatment. A sedative response does not establish effective treatment of core symptoms.

sections.title: Additional referenced study applications
sections.text: A positive PTSD screen is followed by diagnostic assessment; VA/DoD suggests a validated structured clinician interview. Co-occurring substance use disorder alone should not preclude recommended PTSD treatments.

Supportive conversation as the only intervention for every patient
Sleep deprivation
Avoiding any discussion of trauma indefinitely

distractorExplanations.E: Avoidance is not the recommended therapeutic approach.

sections.title: Treat beyond withdrawal
sections.text: Withdrawal-only management is discouraged because relapse and overdose risks remain; offer ongoing medication treatment and support.

sections.title: Know the treatment medications

sections.title: Distinguish rescue from maintenance

sections.title: Additional referenced study applications

sections.title: Treat high fracture risk
sections.text: Postmenopausal women at high fracture risk, especially after a recent fracture, warrant pharmacologic treatment in addition to bone-health measures.

sections.title: Use appropriate initial therapy
sections.text: Bisphosphonates are recommended initial options for high-risk postmenopausal osteoporosis. Reassess risk before considering a bisphosphonate holiday.

sections.title: Do not stop denosumab casually
sections.text: Do not delay or stop denosumab without subsequent therapy to address rebound bone loss and fracture risk. Bisphosphonate holiday rules do not transfer to denosumab.

sections.title: Additional referenced study applications
sections.text: DXA of hip and spine measures bone mineral density and supports osteoporosis assessment. Fracture prevention also includes fall-risk review, safer lighting, secured rugs, and appropriately placed bathroom grab bars. Heel quantitative ultrasound evaluates bone but does not measure BMD; an abnormal result may require DXA assessment.

sections.title: UK comparison: maintain gains after anabolic therapy
sections.text: NOGG’s UK guideline recommends initiating an antiresorptive drug without delay after the approved anabolic-treatment course. Its listed follow-on agents include alendronate, zoledronate and denosumab. This sequence is a fracture-prevention teaching point; suitability and a planned long-term regimen remain necessary. The article’s UK approval durations and intervention thresholds are not presented as United States examination rules.
sections.sourceLocator: Pharmacological treatment options — Anabolic drug treatment, recommendation 13; Summary of main recommendations, follow-on therapy.

sections.title: UK comparison: oral bisphosphonates and esophageal emptying
sections.text: NOGG identifies esophageal abnormalities that delay emptying, such as stricture or achalasia, as contraindications to oral bisphosphonates. Inability to remain upright after the dose is another administration-related contraindication. Oral convenience does not remove these restrictions. Choosing an alternative still requires the separate renal, calcium, safety and preference assessment; this excerpt does not designate one alternative as best for everyone.

sections.title: Use a structured clinical assessment
sections.text: AAOS supports CTS-6 clinical assessment in place of routine ultrasound or electrodiagnostic testing for diagnosis in appropriate adult presentations.

sections.title: Avoid routine MRI for diagnosis
sections.text: AAOS recommends against MRI as a diagnostic test for CTS. Choose testing to resolve the actual clinical question.

sections.title: Counsel about long-term outcomes
sections.text: Corticosteroid injection has not demonstrated long-term improvement of CTS in the guideline evidence; it should not be presented as a reliably lasting cure.

sections.title: Additional referenced study applications
sections.text: CTS involves compression of the median nerve at the wrist and often causes thumb, index, and middle-finger symptoms, sometimes worse at night with bent wrists. Night wrist splinting is a described treatment option. Severe or refractory symptoms may prompt surgical consideration; the summary does not describe acupuncture as proven to improve CTS.

Lumbar puncture
Routine wrist MRI

Ankle-brachial index

distractorExplanations.B: Lumbar puncture is not the CTS assessment.
distractorExplanations.C: MRI is recommended against for CTS diagnosis.
distractorExplanations.E: An ankle index evaluates another system.

distractorExplanations.C: Reassessment may still be needed.
distractorExplanations.D: Nerve regeneration is not the demonstrated result.
distractorExplanations.E: Universal equivalence is unsupported.

distractorExplanations.D: The supplied wrist and finger pattern supports the cited median-nerve explanation.
distractorExplanations.E: The source does not establish this alternative for the described CTS pattern.

sections.title: Combine useful mechanisms
sections.text: Benzoyl peroxide and topical retinoids are strongly supported. Regimens can combine complementary topical mechanisms.

sections.title: Protect antibiotic effectiveness
sections.text: Use benzoyl peroxide with topical or oral antibiotics to reduce resistance risk. Limit systemic antibiotic exposure when feasible.

sections.title: Recognize treatment failure
sections.text: Isotretinoin is recommended for severe acne or acne that has failed standard oral or topical therapy, subject to its separate safety requirements.

sections.title: Additional referenced study applications
sections.text: Acne assessment includes review of current and recently stopped medicines. Supportive skin care uses gentle cleansing and avoids rough scrubbing, squeezing, or picking lesions, which can contribute to scars or dark marks.

Topical acyclovir

Topical lidocaine

sections.title: Support the barrier and control inflammation
sections.text: Moisturizers and topical anti-inflammatory treatment are supported. Choose topical corticosteroid potency and site appropriately rather than applying one regimen everywhere.

sections.title: Reassess before escalating
sections.text: Persistent disease despite treatment warrants reassessment of diagnosis, exposures and adherence. The adult focused update adds selected newer therapies.

sections.title: Apply pediatric guidance deliberately
sections.text: The 2026 pediatric recommendations support moisturizers and appropriate topical treatments and recommend against routine systemic corticosteroids. Check individual drug age indications separately.

sections.title: Additional referenced study applications
sections.text: AD assessment includes possible irritants such as detergents and fragrances and the impact on sleep. Ongoing itch that disrupts rest warrants review of disease control rather than being ignored because the rash appears limited.

Chronic oral prednisone for every localized flare
Topical acyclovir

sections.title: Treat the appropriate site
sections.text: Topical corticosteroids are recommended for plaque psoriasis outside intertriginous areas. Site, potency and duration affect the treatment plan.

sections.title: Consider steroid-sparing treatment
sections.text: Vitamin D analogues and other selected steroid-sparing topicals can contribute to management. Prolonged corticosteroid use requires supervision.

sections.title: Look beyond the skin
sections.text: Assess relevant comorbidities, including psoriatic arthritis and cardiometabolic and mental-health concerns; coordinate care when findings warrant it.

sections.title: Additional referenced study applications
sections.text: Guttate psoriasis can present as small scattered lesions after an upper respiratory infection. Inverse psoriasis appears as smoother patches in skin folds, where rubbing and sweating can worsen symptoms. Plaque psoriasis has raised scaly patches, pustular psoriasis has pustules, and erythrodermic psoriasis has widespread involvement.

questions.stem: An adult has limited plaque psoriasis on the trunk without flexural involvement. Which listed treatment has guideline support for local therapy?

Donepezil
Disulfiram

distractorExplanations.D: Donepezil is not psoriasis treatment.
distractorExplanations.E: Disulfiram is not psoriasis treatment.

sections.title: Cover the likely organism
sections.text: Typical mild nonpurulent cellulitis without systemic illness calls for streptococcal coverage. Oral cephalexin is one suitable option when appropriate.

sections.title: Base extension on response
sections.text: A five-day course is recommended for uncomplicated cellulitis that improves; extend therapy when improvement is insufficient.

sections.title: Reassess concerning presentations
sections.text: Deeper infection concern, severe compromise or failed outpatient care can warrant hospitalization. A purulent collection requires an abscess-specific assessment.

sections.title: Additional referenced study applications
sections.text: Cellulitis affects skin and deeper underlying tissues; skin injury can provide a bacterial entry point. The MedlinePlus summary distinguishes oral antibiotics for mild cases from possible IV antibiotics in more severe cases.

Fluconazole
Cephalexin
Disulfiram
No antibacterial treatment
